 Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

 The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides
 the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial
 system.

 Financial Stability Report - May 2026 

 Financial Stability Report - May 2026

 Please enable JavaScript if it is disabled in your browser or access the information through the links provided below.

 Purpose and Framework 

 Overview 1. Asset Valuations 2. Borrowing by Businesses and Households 3. Leverage in the Financial Sector 4. Funding Risks 5. Near-Term Risks to the Financial System 

 Accessible Version - Financial Stability Report - May 2026

 Overview of financial system vulnerabilities

 Asset valuations 

 The forward equity price-to-earnings ratio remained in the upper ranges of its historical distribution.

 Corporate bond spreads remained low by historical standards. Leveraged loan spreads increased but remain below median levels.

 Treasury term premiums moved higher and liquidity briefly declined during a period of elevated interest rate volatility, but liquidity has since recovered.

 Valuation pressures in residential real estate remained elevated, while commercial real estate prices continued to stabilize.

 Borrowing by businesses and households 

 Total business and household debt relative to gross domestic product continued to decline, falling to levels not seen since the early 2000s.

 Credit quality of investment-grade corporations was robust, while some riskier firms, particularly those relying on private credit, faced challenges in servicing their debt.

 Household balance sheets continued to be strong, with most debt owed by borrowers with strong credit scores. Auto and credit card delinquencies remained at high levels relative to the past decade.

 Overall mortgage delinquency rates stayed low by historical standards, and home equity cushions remained large. That said, delinquencies of Federal Housing Administration loans are above pre-pandemic levels.

 Leverage in the financial sector 

 Hedge fund leverage stayed high and continues to be concentrated in the largest funds.

 The banking system remained sound and resilient, with historically high regulatory capital ratios. Fair value losses on fixed-rate assets improved somewhat but stayed elevated.

 Leverage at the largest life insurers stayed in the top quartile of its historical distribution.

 Dealer leverage stayed low, while their intermediation activity has increased somewhat in recent quarters.

 Funding risks 

 Most domestic banks maintained high levels of liquid assets, and their reliance on uninsured deposits was well below 2023 peaks.

 Life insurers’ nontraditional liabilities continued to grow, although the ratio of those liabilities to general account assets remained small.

 Certain business development companies experienced increased redemptions triggered by concerns about underlying assets, leading some to exercise limits on these redemptions.

 Assets in cash management vehicles continued to grow, primarily driven by historically less-fragile government money market funds.

 Return to text 

 Survey of salient risks to the financial system

 Survey respondents cited several emerging and existing events or conditions as presenting risks to the U.S. financial system and the broader global economy. For more information, see the box "Survey of Salient Risks to Financial Stability."

 Artificial intelligence

 Persistent inflation

 Note: The data begin in October 1991. The figure shows the difference between the aggregate forward earnings-to-price ratio of Standard & Poor’s 500 firms and the expected real Treasury yields, based on expected earnings for 12 months ahead. Expected real Treasury yields are calculated from the 10-year consumer price index inflation forecast, and the smoothed nominal yield curve is estimated from off-the-run securities. Values are reported as of month-end, except for the value of the last month of the series, which is reported as of the data close date. The median value is 4.59 percentage points.

 Figure 1.7. Corporate bond yields rose slightly but remained in line with historical levels

 This is a line chart showing monthly corporate bond yield data from 1997 through April 2026. The y-axis shows percent values ranging from 0 to 24. The chart displays two series: Triple-B (thick blue line) and High-yield (thin black line). The series’ values are volatile, and their patterns mirror each other at different levels. The high-yield bond series ranges from approximately 4 to 22 percent over the period, with significant peaks around 2002 and 2009, reaching about 14 percent and 22 percent respectively. The triple-B bond yield ranges from approximately 3 to 10 percent, with significant peaks around 2002 and 2009, reaching about 8 percent and 10 percent respectively. As of April 2026, the high-yield bond yield is approximately 7 percent, while the triple-B bond yield is about 5 percent.

 Note: The triple-B series reflects the effective yield of the ICE Bank of America Merrill Lynch (BofAML) triple-B U.S. Corporate Index (C0A4), and the high-yield series reflects the effective yield of the ICE BofAML U.S. High Yield Index (H0A0). Values are reported as of month-end, except for the value of the last month of the series, which is reported as of the data close date.

 Source: ICE Data Indices, LLC, used with permission.

 Return to text 

 Figure 1.8. Corporate bond spreads were roughly unchanged and stayed at low levels

 This is a line chart showing monthly corporate bond spread data from 1997 through April 2026. The chart uses dual y-axes: the left axis shows percentage points from 0 to 11 for Triple-B spreads (thick blue line), while the right axis shows percentage points from 0 to 22 for High-yield spreads (thin black line). Both series follow similar patterns throughout the period, with spikes every few years. The most dramatic spike occurs during 2008-2009, when high-yield spreads reached approximately 20 percentage points and triple-B spreads approached 8 percentage points. Other notable increases appear around 2001-2002 and 2020. Throughout most of the period between spikes, spreads fluctuate at lower levels. As of April 2026, high-yield spreads are approximately 3 percentage points and Triple-B spreads are close to 1 percentage point.

 Note: The triple-B series reflects the option-adjusted spread of the ICE Bank of America Merrill Lynch (BofAML) triple-B U.S. Corporate Index (C0A4), and the high-yield series reflects the option-adjusted spread of the ICE BofAML U.S. High Yield Index (H0A0). Values are reported as of month-end, except for the value of the last month of the series, which is reported as of the data close date.

 Source: ICE Data Indices, LLC, used with permission.

 Note: The excess bond premium (EBP) is a measure of bond market investors’ risk sentiment. It is derived as the residual of a regression that models corporate bond spreads after controlling for expected default losses. By construction, its historical mean is 0. Positive (negative) EBP values indicate that investors’ risk appetite is below (above) its historical mean.

 Source: Federal Reserve Board staff calculations based on Lehman Brothers Fixed Income Database (Warga); Intercontinental Exchange, Inc., ICE Data Services; Center for Research in Security Prices, CRSP/Compustat Merged Database, Wharton Research Data Services; S&P Global, Compustat.

 Figure 1.11. Treasury market depth was volatile but, on net, remained mostly unchanged since November

 This is a line chart showing a 5-day moving average of Treasury market depth from January 2019 through April 2026. The chart uses dual y-axes, both measured in millions of dollars: the left scale ranges from 0 to 35 for the 30-year Treasury (thick burgundy line), and the right scale ranges from 0 to 350 for both the 5-year Treasury (thin black line) and 10-year Treasury (medium-thick blue line). All three series show significant volatility throughout the period. Market depth was generally higher in early 2019, with the 5-year Treasury reaching around 250-300 million dollars and the 30-year around 25-30 million dollars. A sharp decline occurred across all maturities in early 2020, with depths dropping to approximately 20 million dollars for 5-year and 10-year Treasuries, and about 5 million dollars for 30-year Treasuries. After recovering somewhat, market depths declined again in 2022-2023 before beginning to recover again. The chart shows a notable drop in April 2025 across all maturities, followed by a recovery throughout the rest of the year. There is a notable increase across all series in January 2026 and volatility through the end of all series in April 2026. As of April 23, 2026, the 30-year depth was approximately 25 million, the 10-year around 150 million, and the 5-year about 100 million dollars.

 Note: Market depth is defined as the average top 3 bid and ask quote sizes for on-the-run Treasury securities.

 Source: Inter Dealer Broker Community.

 Return to text 

 Figure 1.12. Market depth for the most liquid 2-year on-the-run Treasury note stayed at historically low levels

 This is a line chart showing 5-day moving average 2-year Treasury market depth from 2019 to 2026. The y-axis ranges from 0 to 350 millions of dollars. Market depth is plotted as a single black line. The market depth starts around 50 million dollars in 2019, rises significantly through 2020 to peak at about 300 million dollars in early 2021, then drops sharply through 2021 to approximately 50 million dollars by 2022. From 2022 through 2025, the market depth remains relatively flat around 50 million dollars, with only minor fluctuations. As of April 23, 2026, the market depth remains approximately 50 million dollars.

 Note: The data show the time-weighted average market depth at the best quoted prices to buy and sell for 2-year Treasury notes.

 Source: BrokerTec; Federal Reserve Board staff calculations.
